At Wrexham, Hollywood actors Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney have turned a tiny Welsh soccer team into a global phenomenon, reality TV show and a winning machine.

But how did a pair of Hollywood outsiders crack the code that’s flummoxed so many deep-pocketed owners?

AGREEMENT REACHED! The current owners of the Chicago Bears, the McCaskey and Ryan families, have reached a deal to share the equity owned by late investor Andrew McKenna in a transaction that values the NFL team at roughly $8.8 billion, according to multiple people familiar with the matter.

The two families will share the roughly 2% of the team as part of the agreement. After the transaction closes, the McCaskeys will own about 77.5% of the Bears, with the Ryans holding the rest.

Wrexham AFC’s Dazzling Ascent: Premier League in Sight?

Wrexham AFC, now a Championship club after three straight promotions, has sparked feverish excitement about a possible Premier League leap in 2026. Guided by Hollywood owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney, the Red Dragons are leveraging bold transfer spending and smart financial strategies to fuel their meteoric rise, with their global brand generating unprecedented revenue.

Since the 2021 takeover, Wrexham’s finances have soared. Their 2023-24 accounts reported £26.7 million in revenue, surpassing many Championship rivals, with £13.18 million from commercial deals, £5 million from matchdays, and £4.45 million from retail, according to BBC Sport. This financial firepower, amplified by sponsorships and the “Welcome to Wrexham” documentary’s worldwide appeal, enables hefty transfer investments while staying within Profitability and Sustainability Rules. Experts like Kieran Maguire estimate a £150 million valuation post promotion, a 7,400% surge from the £2 million purchase price.

This summer, Wrexham splashed out £7.5 million on Ipswich Town’s Nathan Broadhead and Sheffield United’s Kieffer Moore, a club record, per The Wrexham Insider. Manager Phil Parkinson continues targeting attacking talent, with interest in Bournemouth’s Daniel Jebbison and Wolves’ Craig Dawson. Despite a £25 million transfer budget, fan pundit Liam noted that stadium upgrades, like the new Kop Stand at STōK Cae Ras to meet UEFA standards, may cap spending at £5-6 million. The expanded 18,000 capacity stadium reflects their lofty ambitions.

The Championship poses challenges, with average wages (£12,000/week) far exceeding League One’s (£2,500/week) and parachute payment clubs outspending Wrexham’s £11 million wage bill. Yet, with £8 million in projected TV revenue and growing sponsorships, their financial model supports bold moves. As Wrexham face Southampton in their Championship opener on August 9th, their mix of star power, strategic investments, and passionate fanbase makes a Premier League dream thrillingly attainable.
